```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

# The benchmark needs a timer (bench) and the comparison backend (a real
# BSgenome forged from the bundled FASTA, which requires BSgenome,
# rtracklayer, and Biostrings). When any are missing, the prose and code
# still render but the timed chunks are skipped so the vignette knits
# everywhere (CRAN/Bioc, the docs site, a bare R install).
run_bench <- requireNamespace("bench", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("BSgenome", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("rtracklayer", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("Biostrings", quietly = TRUE)

have_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

BiocRefgetStore exposes a BSgenome-compatible interface to sequences backed by
a [refget](https://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/refget.html) store (via the
Rust-backed `gtars` crate). This vignette is a how-to for deciding **which
backend to reach for** when you extract sequence: the RefgetStore backend in
this package (`RefgetGenome`) or the classic Bioconductor stack
(`BSgenome::getSeq()` on a real `BSgenome` object).

It is not a table of pre-baked numbers. Every figure below is produced *at knit
time* by the package's own benchmark harness (`run_benchmarks()`, defined in
`R/benchmark.R`) running on a small synthetic genome bundled in the package. So
the absolute times depend on the machine that built this page, but the *shape*
of the comparison is stable and reproducible.

## The two backends

**RefgetGenome (this package).** Built from a FASTA, a directory store, or a
remote refget store. Sequences are addressed by digest, and the bulk extraction
path (`extractRegions()`) hands an entire region set to Rust in a single
foreign-function call, so per-region R overhead does not accumulate. See
[Getting Started](getting-started.html) for construction details.

**BSgenome (the comparator).** The long-standing Bioconductor representation of
a genome. `BSgenome::getSeq()` reads from an on-disk `2bit` blob memory-mapped
into the session. Whole-chromosome and in-memory access are its sweet spot.

To make the comparison apples-to-apples, the harness forges a **real**
in-memory `BSgenome` object from *the same FASTA* the RefgetStore reads (no
data-package install, no network). Both backends therefore see identical
seqnames and coordinates, and the harness asserts that the extracted sequences
match (the `check` column below). An indexed-FASTA `Rsamtools::FaFile` is
included as a secondary baseline when Rsamtools is available.

## Running the benchmark

The whole comparison is one call. `run_benchmarks()` builds the contestants
from the bundled FASTA, warms each one (so index loads and mmap faults are
excluded from timing), times single-region, bulk multi-region, and
full-chromosome extraction, and returns a tidy data frame.

```{r run, eval = run_bench}
library(BiocRefgetStore)

fa <- system.file("extdata/benchmark/bench_genome.fa",
                  package = "BiocRefgetStore")

# Smaller bulk set + iteration count keeps knit-time modest; the defaults
# (n_bulk = 1000) are what you'd use for a real measurement.
results <- run_benchmarks(fa, n_bulk = 200, min_iterations = 5)
str(results)
```

```{r run-fallback, eval = !run_bench, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("> **Benchmark not run.** `bench`, `BSgenome`, `rtracklayer`, or",
    "`Biostrings` is not installed, so the timed chunks are skipped.",
    "Install those Suggests to reproduce the tables and plot below.\n")
```

The returned data frame has one row per (operation, backend): `operation`
(`single` / `bulk` / `full_chrom`), `backend` (`bsgenome` / `refget` /
`fafile`), `n_regions`, `total_bp`, `median_time` (seconds), `mem_alloc`,
`iterations`, and `check` (did this backend's output match the reference?).

## Timing results

We format the live `results` into a readable table: median time in
milliseconds, throughput in megabases per second, and the cross-backend
correctness flag.

```{r table, eval = run_bench}
tab <- results
tab$median_ms <- round(tab$median_time * 1e3, 3)
tab$mb_per_s <- round((tab$total_bp / 1e6) / tab$median_time, 1)
tab <- tab[order(tab$operation, tab$median_time),
           c("operation", "backend", "n_regions", "total_bp",
             "median_ms", "mb_per_s", "check")]

knitr::kable(
  tab,
  col.names = c("Operation", "Backend", "N regions", "Total bp",
                "Median (ms)", "MB/s", "Match"),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Median extraction time by operation and backend (lower is faster)."
)
```

## Comparison plot

```{r plot, eval = run_bench && have_ggplot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(results, aes(x = backend, y = median_time * 1e3, fill = backend)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ operation, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median time (ms)",
       title = "Extraction time by backend, faceted by operation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

```{r plot-fallback, eval = run_bench && !have_ggplot, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("> *ggplot2 is not installed; skipping the plot.* The table above carries",
    "the same information.\n")
```

## How to read this

The interesting comparison is not a single winner but *where each backend
wins*:

- **Bulk multi-region extraction** (`bulk`) is the headline case for
  RefgetStore. `extractRegions()` passes the whole region set across the FFI
  boundary once, so it avoids the per-region R-level overhead that the
  `getSeq(bsgenome, gr)` path pays as the region count grows. This is the
  workload to watch in the table above.
- **Full-chromosome extraction** (`full_chrom`) plays to BSgenome's strength:
  once the `2bit` is mapped, returning a whole contiguous sequence is close to
  a memory read.
- **Single-region extraction** (`single`) is dominated by fixed per-call
  overhead in both backends, so the numbers are small and noisy; don't
  over-read them.

There is also a one-time **setup cost** that the harness deliberately excludes
from timing: constructing the RefgetGenome store, indexing the FASTA, or
forging/loading the BSgenome. If you only ever read one region, that setup cost
dominates everything in the table.

### Which backend should I use?

- **Pick RefgetGenome** for many-region or streaming workloads (BED-driven bulk
  extraction), remote/on-demand access where you don't want the whole genome
  on disk, and digest-addressed reproducibility.
- **Pick BSgenome** when you already have the data package installed and your
  work is mostly whole-chromosome, in-memory access.

See the [Reference](reference.html) vignette for the complete API.

## Optional: benchmarking against a real genome

The same harness runs against a real assembly by naming an installed BSgenome
data package and pointing `fasta_path` at that genome's FASTA (so coordinates
match). This is **not run** when the vignette knits -- it needs a multi-hundred-
megabyte data package and is gated behind an environment variable so a
developer can opt in without editing this file.

```{r real-genome, eval = nzchar(Sys.getenv("REFGET_BENCH_REAL")) && requireNamespace("BSgenome.Scerevisiae.UCSC.sacCer3", quietly = TRUE)}
# Opt in with: Sys.setenv(REFGET_BENCH_REAL = "1")
# and an installed BSgenome data package + matching FASTA.
res_real <- run_benchmarks(
  fasta_path = "sacCer3.fa",
  bsgenome_pkg = "BSgenome.Scerevisiae.UCSC.sacCer3",
  n_bulk = 1000
)
knitr::kable(res_real)
```

For a full human assembly the pattern is identical: install
`BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38`, supply its FASTA, and on the RefgetStore side
build from an on-disk or remote store via `RefgetGenome.from_directory()` or
`RefgetGenome.from_remote()` (see [Getting Started](getting-started.html)).
